spatial_entity.notes: Polity slice limited to 600–539 BCE for which Cliopatria geometry and evidence are both available.

claim.summary: Slavery was an established institution in Neo-Babylonian urban society. Specialist scholarship finds ownership concentrated among elites, with some wealthy families holding very large numbers of enslaved people; slave labour was not the cheapest or dominant labour source, but it played an important role in entrepreneurial management. Surviving Babylonian tablets directly document slave sales.

territorial_practice.notes: P3 denotes a strongly supported institutional practice without treating Babylonia as a slave society comparable to classical Athens or Rome.

source.title: Babylonia: The Seventh–Fifth Centuries BC
source.independence_notes: Specialist comparative study of Babylonian slave systems.
source.reliability_limitations: Elite archives overrepresent propertied urban households; slave labour's wider demographic share remains different from its visibility in business archives.

source.title: Cuneiform tablet: slave sale, Egibi archive
source.independence_notes: Museum catalogue record for a Neo-Babylonian slave-sale tablet.
source.reliability_limitations: One transaction proves a bounded sale, not prevalence by itself.
